name: Namobuddha
tagline: Hilltop stupa and Tibetan monastery on the tigress legend site
meta_description: Namobuddha guide: the tigress stupa, Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery, morning prayers, meditation, hikes from Dhulikhel and how to reach from Kathmandu.
summary: Namobuddha is a Buddhist pilgrimage hill at about 1,750 m in Kavre district, roughly 40 km south-east of Kathmandu. A stupa marks where, in the Jataka tale, a prince gave his body to a starving tigress, and the large Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery crowns the ridge above. Most visitors base in Dhulikhel, 45 minutes away.
intro: Namobuddha is one of the three great stupa sites of the Kathmandu Valley region for Tibetan Buddhists, alongside Boudhanath and Swayambhunath, yet it sees a small fraction of their visitors. The reason is distance: it lies beyond the valley rim, on a forested ridge above the Kavre hills, and the last stretch of road is slow. That remoteness is the appeal. Mornings here belong to monks chanting in the assembly hall, prayer flags cracking in the wind, and terraced farmland falling away on every side toward a long line of Himalaya.

The site rests on a Jataka story, one of the tales of the Buddha's earlier lives. Prince Mahasattva, out walking with his brothers, found a tigress so weak from hunger that she could not feed her five cubs. He offered his own body so that they could live. The white stupa in the village below the ridge is said to hold his relics, and a stone relief on the hilltop marks the spot where the offering took place. Tibetans call the place Takmo Lujin, the tigress body-gift.

Above the relief rises the Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery, founded by Khenchen Thrangu Rinpoche of the Karma Kagyu tradition and opened in its present form in 2008. Over 250 monks study and live here, with a monastic college, a school for young monks and a Tibetan medicine clinic. We bring guests for a day from Dhulikhel, or for one or two quiet nights, usually between October and April, when skies are clearer and paths dry.
facts: ≈ 40 km · 2–2.5 h by road via Dhulikhel
Tigress Jataka stupa, Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery, meditation

highlights.title: Morning prayers with 250 monks
highlights.text: The main assembly hall of Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery fills for chanting at dawn and again in the late afternoon, with horns, drums and cymbals marking the rhythm. Visitors may sit quietly at the back. Timings follow the monastic calendar, so we confirm them on the day.

highlights.title: The tigress relief on the hilltop
highlights.text: A short climb from the village leads to a stone relief showing Prince Mahasattva offering himself to the starving tigress and her cubs, marking the spot named in the Jataka tale. Pilgrims leave butter lamps and white khata scarves here, and the whole hillside is strung with thousands of prayer flags.

highlights.title: The relic stupa in the village
highlights.text: Below the ridge, a whitewashed stupa with painted eyes stands among village houses and is said to enshrine the prince's relics. Pilgrims walk clockwise around it spinning prayer wheels. It is smaller than Boudhanath but older in story, and early-morning light from the east falls straight onto the dome.

highlights.title: Himalayan views across the Kavre hills
highlights.text: From the monastery terraces, clear mornings between October and February show a line of snow peaks to the north and north-east, including Dorje Lakpa and the Langtang range, with Gauri Shankar further east. Below lie terraced fields and Tamang and Newar villages scattered across the ridges.

highlights.title: Quiet for meditation
highlights.text: At night Namobuddha is silent apart from wind and dogs; there is no traffic, and the nearest town is 8 km downhill. That stillness is why retreat groups come here. Short guided sessions are easy to arrange, and longer teachings at the monastery take place for registered participants on set dates.

highlights.title: Ridge walks to Dhulikhel and Panauti
highlights.text: Namobuddha sits at the end of a classic day hike from Dhulikhel, three to four hours through farmland and pine forest. From the monastery, a two to three hour walk drops 8 km to Panauti, the old Newar town on the river, where the car can collect you.

how_to_reach.text: From Kathmandu, drive ≈ 30 km east on the Araniko Highway to Dhulikhel in 1–1.5 hours, then ≈ 13 km south on a narrower hill road to Namobuddha, another 40–50 minutes. Allow 2–2.5 hours in total. A few local buses run from Dhulikhel and Panauti, but timings are irregular, so most visitors use a private car or a taxi from Dhulikhel.

The most popular approach is the hike from Dhulikhel: about 3–4 hours each way along ridges, through villages and pine forest, with a net climb of roughly 200 m. Walkers often return by car, or continue downhill to Panauti in 2–3 hours and drive back from there.

Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu is the nearest airport, ≈ 40 km and about 2 hours by car. Arriving guests heading straight to a retreat can drive directly from the airport via Bhaktapur and Dhulikhel without entering central Kathmandu.

where_to_stay: Dhulikhel, 13 km and 45 minutes away, is the usual base, with mountain-view hotels such as Dhulikhel Mountain Resort and an old town for the evening. Staying right at Namobuddha is quieter. The monastery runs a simple guesthouse for visitors and retreat participants, which often fills, so book well ahead through the monastery's own channels. Namo Buddha Resort, a small cottage resort a short walk from the monastery, has offered rooms and vegetarian meals in a garden setting; confirm availability when booking. Village homestays also operate. Panauti, 8 km downhill, has a few guesthouses and suits travellers who plan to hike up in the morning.
tips: Walk clockwise around the stupa, the relief and the monastery buildings, and never step over prayer flags or ritual objects.
Ask before photographing monks, and keep cameras away from the assembly hall during prayers unless a monk tells you it is fine.
There is no entrance fee at Namobuddha, but a donation at the monastery or for butter lamps is customary; check current status before you travel.
Bring a warm jacket even in spring and autumn, as the ridge drops to around 0–5 °C on winter nights and wind is common.
Book the monastery guesthouse or nearby lodges early for October and November, when retreat groups and pilgrims fill the rooms.

experiences.title: Morning prayers at Thrangu Tashi Yangtse
experiences.image_query: Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery Namo Buddha
experiences.summary: Sit at the back of the assembly hall of Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery as more than 250 monks chant their morning prayers, then walk the monastery terraces and shrine rooms with a guide who explains the Karma Kagyu tradition, the murals and the daily routine of monastic life.
body: Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery was founded by Khenchen Thrangu Rinpoche, a senior teacher of the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, and opened in its present form in December 2008. Its red-and-gold buildings stretch along the top of the ridge, with a main assembly hall, a monastic college for advanced study, a school for young monks and a Tibetan medicine clinic. Seen from the road below, it looks larger than the hill should allow.

Prayers begin early, often around dawn, and again in the late afternoon. Inside, rows of monks in maroon robes sit facing each other, with long horns, drums and cymbals punctuating the chant. Visitors enter quietly, remove shoes, sit on cushions at the back or along the sides, and stay for as long as they like; leaving in a gap between chants is polite. Young monks may be shy or curious, and the older ones often wave newcomers to a better spot.

After prayers, your guide walks you through the shrine hall, its tall Buddha images and wall paintings, and out onto the terraces for the Himalayan view. Photography rules vary between rooms, so watch for signs and ask; flash is never welcome. There is no entrance fee, though donations support the monks' food and schooling. Prayer times shift with the season and the monastic calendar, and the monastery occasionally closes areas for retreats; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend prayers at Namobuddha monastery?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors are welcome to sit quietly at the back of the assembly hall during morning and afternoon prayers at Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery. Remove your shoes, dress modestly, switch off phones and avoid photography unless clearly permitted. Times follow the monastic calendar, so we confirm them on the day of your visit.

faqs.q: What time are prayers at Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery?
faqs.a: Monks usually chant early in the morning, around dawn, and again in the late afternoon, but exact times vary with the season and the monastic calendar. Special ceremonies can run for hours. If you want to see morning prayers, staying overnight at Namobuddha or leaving Dhulikhel by 5.30 am is the practical way.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Namobuddha monastery?
faqs.a: No. At our last visit there was no entrance fee for Namobuddha or the Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery. Donations are welcome and support the monks' food, school and clinic, and many visitors offer butter lamps at the stupa. Arrangements can change, so check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Tigress stupa and prayer flag hill walk
experiences.price_hint: Included in our Dhulikhel and Namobuddha tours
experiences.summary: A walking circuit of the Namobuddha pilgrimage sites: the relic stupa in the village, the stairway through prayer flags to the hilltop relief of the prince and the tigress, and the kora path around the hill, with the Jataka story told stop by stop.
body: We start at the white stupa in the village, where pilgrims spin the prayer wheels set into its base and circle clockwise, some reciting mantras on their beads. Your guide tells the Jataka tale here: three princes walking in the forest, a tigress too starved to feed her five cubs, and the youngest prince, Mahasattva, who cut himself so she would smell blood and then gave her his body. Buddhists teach that this prince was the Buddha in an earlier life, and the stupa is said to hold his relics.

From the stupa, a stone stairway climbs about 15 minutes through dense strings of prayer flags to the hilltop shrine, where a carved stone relief shows the prince lying before the tigress and cubs. Pilgrims light butter lamps, leave white khata scarves and add their own flags; you can buy both at stalls near the top for a few hundred rupees. The monastery buildings rise immediately above, and the views from here reach north to the Himalaya on clear mornings.

The walk finishes with the kora, the circuit path that loops around the hill past chortens, mani stones and more flags. The full circuit is about 2 km with roughly 100 m of climbing, easy for most visitors but stepped in places, so take care with young children and wet stones. Sunrise and the hour before sunset bring the softest light on the flags and the fewest day visitors. There is no fee for any part of the walk; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the story of Namo Buddha?
faqs.a: Namo Buddha marks a Jataka tale in which Prince Mahasattva, an earlier life of the Buddha, found a tigress starving with her five cubs and offered his own body so they could survive. The village stupa is said to hold his relics, and a stone relief on the hilltop marks where the offering happened. Tibetans call the site Takmo Lujin.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see Namobuddha?
faqs.a: Allow two to three hours for the stupa, the hilltop relief, the kora path and a visit to the monastery. With the drive from Kathmandu, a day trip takes six to seven hours. If you want to attend morning prayers or meditate, stay one night at Namobuddha or nearby Dhulikhel.

faqs.q: Can I hang prayer flags at Namobuddha?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors may add prayer flags on the hill, and stalls near the stupa and the hilltop sell sets for a few hundred rupees. Tie them high where they can catch the wind, never on trees that are already overloaded, and do not cut or remove existing flags. Your guide can explain the meaning of the five colours.

experiences.title: Guided meditation session at Namobuddha
experiences.summary: A guided session of breathing and sitting meditation on the Namobuddha ridge, led by an experienced teacher and suited to complete beginners. It sits well after morning prayers at the monastery and forms the core of our yoga and meditation retreat days.
body: Namobuddha's quiet makes it one of the easiest places near Kathmandu to try meditation for the first time. We arrange sessions with experienced local meditation teachers, held in a quiet room or garden at your lodge or near the monastery, depending on where you stay and the season. The monastery itself hosts teachings and retreats for registered participants on set dates; a short visitor session is separate from that programme and needs no prior experience.

A typical session runs 90 minutes. It opens with an explanation of posture and simple breathing practice, moves to two or three short periods of sitting meditation of 10 to 20 minutes each, and closes with walking meditation outdoors and time for questions. Teachers draw on the Tibetan Buddhist approach practised at the monastery, but the instructions are practical and non-religious, so guests of any faith or none take part comfortably. Cushions and mats are provided; chairs are available for anyone with stiff knees.

Early morning after prayers and the hour before dark are the stillest times, and the ridge stays cool, so bring a fleece and a shawl. We schedule one or two sessions a day on our five-night yoga and meditation retreat, which spends two nights here and two in Dhulikhel. Costs depend on group size and teacher; around ₹3,000 per person is typical for a private session including the teacher's travel. Teacher availability shifts with monastery events and festivals, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: Yes. Our guided sessions at Namobuddha are designed for complete beginners, starting with posture and breathing before short sitting periods of 10 to 20 minutes. Teachers explain everything in plain English and adapt for stiff knees or back problems, with chairs available. No religious belief or prior practice is needed to take part.

faqs.q: Does Namobuddha monastery offer meditation retreats?
faqs.a: The Thrangu Tashi Yangtse Monastery hosts teachings and retreats on set dates for registered participants, and its retreat centres serve committed practitioners. For travellers on a shorter schedule, we arrange private guided sessions with a teacher at your lodge or near the monastery. Programmes and dates change each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days should I spend at Namobuddha for a retreat?
faqs.a: Two nights is a good minimum: it allows an evening session, morning prayers, a full day of practice and a second dawn. Our five-night yoga and meditation retreat spends two nights at Namobuddha and two in Dhulikhel, with one night in Kathmandu, which balances quiet practice with gentle hikes and views.

faqs.q: How far is Namobuddha from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Namobuddha is about 40 km south-east of Kathmandu by road, a drive of 2 to 2.5 hours via the Araniko Highway to Dhulikhel and then a hill road for the last 13 km. From Dhulikhel it takes about 45 minutes by car, or three to four hours on foot along the ridge.

faqs.q: Can I do Namobuddha as a day trip from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes. Leave Kathmandu by 7 am, reach Namobuddha by about 9.30 am, spend two to three hours at the stupa and monastery, and return via Panauti or Dhulikhel for lunch. You will be back in Kathmandu by late afternoon. It is a long day, so we often suggest a night in Dhulikhel instead.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Namobuddha?
faqs.a: October to April is best. October and November bring the clearest Himalayan views and dry paths; December to February are clear but cold, with nights near 0 °C; March and April are warmer, with rhododendrons and some haze. June to September brings monsoon rain, mist and leeches on the hiking trails.

faqs.q: Is Namobuddha worth visiting if I have seen Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Yes, because it offers what Boudhanath cannot: silence, countryside and a working monastery of over 250 monks without city crowds. The tigress legend, the prayer-flag hill and the mountain views make it a different experience altogether. Visitors interested in Tibetan Buddhism often say it was the highlight of their time in the valley.

faqs.q: Where should I stay when visiting Namobuddha?
faqs.a: Most visitors stay in Dhulikhel, 45 minutes away, at hotels such as Dhulikhel Mountain Resort. For a quieter night, the monastery guesthouse and Namo Buddha Resort are close to the hilltop, and village homestays operate nearby. Panauti, 8 km downhill, has a few guesthouses for walkers starting early.

faqs.q: How hard is the Dhulikhel to Namobuddha hike?
faqs.a: It is an easy to moderate day hike of about 3 to 4 hours one way, following ridges, village tracks and pine forest from Dhulikhel at 1,550 m to Namobuddha at about 1,750 m. Some stretches are dusty dirt road. Most people walk one way and return by car or continue downhill to Panauti.

faqs.q: What should I wear at Namobuddha monastery?
faqs.a: Wear clothes that cover shoulders and knees, and shoes that slip off easily, as you will remove them before entering shrine rooms. Avoid hats inside, and pack a warm layer, since the hilltop is windy and cool year round. Bright, revealing clothing draws attention in a place where monks live and study.

faqs.q: Is Namobuddha suitable for elderly travellers?
faqs.a: Mostly, yes. Cars reach the village near the stupa, and the monastery can be reached with a short climb on steps. The hilltop relief involves about 15 minutes of stairs, which most seniors manage at their own pace with rests. The road from Dhulikhel is narrow and winding, so travellers prone to car sickness should sit in front.

Buddha Jayanti, the full moon of April or May, and Losar, the Tibetan New Year in February or March, draw pilgrims and special ceremonies at the monastery. Local fairs are also held around the stupa on certain full moons. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel if you hope to coincide with one.
